stories.original:
**Stripe agrees $7bn deal for AI gateway firm OpenRouter**

*Acquiring a key routing layer for AI model access would extend Stripe's infrastructure play well beyond payments.*

Stripe is acquiring OpenRouter, an AI gateway platform that routes requests across multiple large language models, for $7 billion, according to Bloomberg. The deal would represent Stripe's largest acquisition by a wide margin, dwarfing its $1.1 billion purchase of Bridge in 2024.

OpenRouter acts as middleware between developers and AI model providers, handling authentication, billing and model selection. For Stripe, which already processes payments for AI-native businesses and recently built a payment layer for AI agents with AWS, the acquisition would embed it deeper into the commercial infrastructure of AI. Controlling the gateway through which developers access and pay for AI models places Stripe between buyers and sellers at the point of transaction – the same position it occupies in payments.

The deal points to a broader convergence between payments infrastructure and AI orchestration. As agentic commerce moves from prototype to production, the firms that control authentication, billing and settlement layers for machine-to-machine interactions are the same ones positioned to process the resulting transaction flows. Stripe is paying $7 billion for a routing layer – a price that reflects how directly the largest payments companies now see AI orchestration as an extension of their core business.

*Sources: [Stripe agrees $7bn takeover of AI firm OpenRouter - Bloomberg](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48258/stripe-agrees-7bn-takeover-of-ai-firm-openrouter---bloomberg?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*
stories.edited:
**Stripe agrees $7bn acquisition of AI gateway OpenRouter**

*The deal will extend Stripe's infrastructure ambitions beyond payments, giving it control of the routing layer through which developers connect applications to LLMs.*

Stripe is acquiring OpenRouter, the AI model gateway, for $7 billion, according to Bloomberg. OpenRouter acts as an intermediary that lets developers route API calls to competing large language models through a single integration, a function analogous to what Stripe itself does for payment methods.

The acquisition follows Stripe's earlier moves into AI-adjacent infrastructure, including its joint bid with Advent for PayPal, its partnership with AWS to build a payment layer for AI agents and its $1 billion purchase of billing platform Metronome in December 2025. Owning a model-routing layer would position Stripe at the intersection of AI compute and commerce, letting it capture billing and metering revenue as AI-native applications scale.

For European payment providers and fintechs building on or competing with Stripe, the next battleground is not just payment rails but the infrastructure layer connecting AI systems to commercial transactions. If AI agents increasingly initiate purchases, the firm that controls both the routing of model calls and the payment execution has a structural advantage.

*Sources: [Stripe agrees $7bn takeover of AI firm OpenRouter - Bloomberg](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48258/stripe-agrees-7bn-takeover-of-ai-firm-openrouter---bloomberg?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**ECB data shows businesses still prefer cash over digital payments**

*Fresh survey findings challenge the assumption that the pandemic permanently shifted European businesses toward digital-only acceptance.*

The European Central Bank has published new data showing that the decline in cash acceptance observed during and after the Covid-19 pandemic has stalled. Businesses across the euro area continue to prefer cash as a payment method, reversing expectations that digital payment adoption would follow a one-way trajectory.

The findings arrive as the ECB advances its digital euro programme, with the European Parliament voting in July to move the legislation to final negotiations and 36 payment providers selected for the pilot phase. A persistent preference for cash among businesses complicates the narrative that a central bank digital currency would meet unmet demand. The instant payments regulation assumes growing digital payment volumes will justify the compliance costs banks face ahead of the 2027 deadline, an assumption the data calls into question.

Merchant behaviour in much of Europe remains stubbornly analogue, despite years of investment in account-to-account and card-based digital payments by processors and fintechs. Product strategies premised on rapid cash displacement may need to account for a longer transition than anticipated.

*Sources: [Companies prefer cash over digital payments - ECB](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48255/companies-prefer-cash-over-digital-payments---ecb?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*
stories.edited:
**ECB data shows businesses still prefer cash over digital payments**

*The decline in cash acceptance among euro area businesses has stalled, challenging assumptions that underpin initiatives from Wero to the digital euro.*

A new ECB survey shows that cash acceptance among euro area businesses, which dropped sharply during the Covid-19 pandemic, has stabilised rather than continuing to fall. Companies across the region continue to prefer cash as a payment method, contradicting the narrative that digital payment adoption is on a one-way trajectory.

The findings arrive as policymakers push competing agendas. The ECB's digital euro project, still in its preparation phase ahead of an operational pilot expected in the second half of 2027, is premised partly on the idea that cash use is declining and a public digital alternative is needed. Simultaneously, the European Payments Initiative's Wero is expanding across European markets as a digital wallet for real-time payments. Both initiatives assume growing consumer and merchant appetite for non-cash instruments.

For payment providers and scheme operators, the data complicates the business case for displacing cash at the point of sale. If merchant preference for cash proves sticky rather than transitional, the adoption curve for pay-by-bank, wallets and the digital euro is likely to be slower than projected, particularly among smaller businesses where cash handling costs are lower relative to digital payment fees.

*Sources: [Companies prefer cash over digital payments - ECB](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48255/companies-prefer-cash-over-digital-payments---ecb?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**Non-euro banks face tightening timeline on instant payments readiness**

*Preparation gaps risk leaving some institutions unable to meet the early 2027 receive obligation, with practical consequences for cross-border settlement reliability.*

A detailed assessment published by Global Banking & Finance Review examines the readiness of non-euro area banks for the next phase of the EU's instant payments regulation. Banks outside the eurozone that offer euro-denominated payment services must be able to receive instant payments by early 2027, with send capability following shortly after, and the analysis suggests that many are not yet on track.

The regulation, which took effect for eurozone banks in stages through 2025 and 2026, extends to non-euro EU member states and EEA participants on a slightly delayed timeline. Banks in countries such as Sweden, Denmark, Poland and Romania must connect to the TIPS infrastructure or an equivalent interoperable system. Iceland's decision in June to sign an agreement to join TIPS – with the system taking effect in 2028 – illustrated one approach, but the operational and liquidity management challenges remain substantial for institutions that have not historically processed euro instant payments at volume.

For payment service providers and corporate treasury teams operating across European borders, the uneven pace of readiness creates practical risks. A transaction that settles instantly in one jurisdiction but queues in another undermines the reliability that the regulation is designed to guarantee.

*Sources: [Instant Euro Payments 2027: Bank Readiness](https://www.globalbankingandfinance.com/instant-euro-payments-2027-non-euro-bank-readiness/) — Global Banking & Finance Review*

**Ingenico secures €150m from Pimco-led investors to reset capital structure**

*Fresh capital provides financial headroom after a prolonged period of ownership uncertainty and competitive pressure from software-based acceptance.*

Ingenico has agreed a capital structure reset anchored by a €150 million investment from a group of global investors led by Pimco. The fresh capital is intended to stabilise the company's balance sheet after years of transition since its take-private by Apollo Funds in 2022.

The terminal industry is under pressure from multiple directions. Software-based acceptance, including tap-to-pay on smartphones, is eroding demand for dedicated hardware, while integrated payment platforms such as Adyen and Stripe offer merchants end-to-end solutions that bypass traditional terminal economics.

The investment suggests Ingenico's backers see enough remaining value in its installed base and enterprise relationships to justify recapitalisation rather than sale or wind-down. European merchants and acquirers depend on Ingenico as a significant provider of in-store acceptance infrastructure across the region, making its financial stability a material consideration for the physical payments supply chain.

*Sources: [Ingenico secures €150 million in fresh capital](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110649/ingenico-secures-150-million-in-fresh-capital?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**Commercial Bank of Dubai launches multi-bank payment initiation under open finance framework**

*Letting customers pay from accounts at other banks through a single app marks a concrete step for the UAE's open finance regime, with parallels to European payment initiation models.*

Commercial Bank of Dubai (CBD) has become the first bank in the UAE to offer multi-bank payment initiation through its mobile app, allowing customers to trigger payments from accounts held at other institutions. The feature operates under the UAE central bank's Open Finance Initiative, the regulation for which was published in mid-2024, with the framework moving into a live environment in December 2025.

The UAE's open finance framework draws directly on lessons from the Payment Services Directive 2 and the UK's open banking model, but is being implemented with broader scope from the outset. Where European regulators are still debating how far beyond payment accounts open finance should extend, the UAE framework already encompasses a wider range of financial products. CBD's implementation of payment initiation through a bank-owned app, rather than through a third-party provider, also inverts the dynamic seen in most European markets, where fintechs have driven adoption.

For European firms with Middle Eastern operations or ambitions, the UAE's approach offers a live comparison point. The speed of implementation, from regulation to production between mid-2024 and December 2025, contrasts with the multi-year timelines that have characterised European open banking and open finance policy.

*Sources: [Commercial Bank of Dubai Becomes First UAE Bank to Launch Multi-Bank Payment Initiation](https://ffnews.com/news/commercial-bank-of-dubai-becomes-first-uae-bank-to-launch-multi-bank-payment-initiation) — Ffnews | [Open Finance UAE: CBD app pays from other banks' accounts](https://tbreak.com/cbd-open-finance-uae-mobile-app-payments/) — Tbreak | [CBD advances open finance in the UAE](https://www.zawya.com/en/press-release/companies-news/cbd-advances-open-finance-in-the-uae-458552) — ZAWYA | [CBD app lets customers make payments from accounts held with other banks](https://gulfnews.com/business/banking/cbd-app-lets-customers-make-payments-from-accounts-held-with-other-banks-1.500643437) — Gulf News*
stories.edited:
**Thunes and Fiserv partner on cross-border merchant payouts**

*The collaboration connects Thunes's cross-border payment network to Fiserv's merchant ecosystem, targeting platforms and marketplaces that need to settle with international sellers.*

Thunes is partnering with Fiserv to handle international payouts for global platforms and marketplaces within Fiserv's merchant ecosystem. The arrangement allows merchants and sellers connected through Fiserv to receive cross-border disbursements via Thunes's network, which covers more than 140 countries through direct connections to mobile wallets, bank accounts and card networks.

Cross-border payouts for marketplace sellers remain a fragmented and operationally complex segment. Most large acquirers and payment service providers handle the inbound collection side but rely on third parties for outbound disbursements, particularly in emerging markets where local payment methods dominate. Thunes has built its business specifically on this outbound corridor, competing with Payoneer, Hyperwallet (PayPal) and Airwallex.

European platforms operating global marketplaces stand to benefit directly, given Fiserv processes a substantial volume of European merchant transactions. Reduced settlement times and costs for cross-border seller payouts would shape how European marketplace operators choose their payment stack.

*Sources: [Thunes to support payouts for Fiserv's merchant ecosystem](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110653/thunes-to-support-payouts-for-fiservs-merchant-ecosystem?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*
